memories.content: Link expected participant burden in each user study task to its corresponding mitigation strategy.
Specify the accommodations necessary for participants to access the prototype and research tasks.
Specify how accessibility accommodations will be provided during user study sessions.
Describe how personal identifiers will be separated from research data immediately after collection.
Specify the equipment to be loaned to participants who lack necessary devices.
Describe the procedure for returning equipment loaned to participants.
HCI ethics reviewers verify that expected burdens and mitigation strategies correspond to each user study task.
Inform participants that the formative evaluation prototype is not a finished service.
Set an upper limit on cumulative task burden when requesting repeated evaluations from the same participant.
The author of this proposal tends to emphasize expected benefits of the prototype over participant burden.
In organizations where leaders or institutional staff handle recruitment, recruitment authority and academic or professional evaluation authority may be combined in the same role.
Specify a single representative measure that will drive operational decisions to maintain, modify, or discontinue the deployed design.
The HCI review panel verifies whether operational decisions can be made based on the declared primary measure.
Establish decision thresholds indicating at what levels key metrics trigger maintaining, modifying, or discontinuing the design.
Evaluate whether reducing workload for one role creates new tasks for other roles through the proposed design changes.
Distinguish usability from organizational adoption intent as separate evaluation outcomes.
Implementation fidelity indicates whether planned features and operational procedures were delivered in the field according to intended specifications.
Initial evaluations and long-term operation do not share identical measurement conditions due to differences in system exposure duration and frequency of repeated use.

analysis.overview: The frames address complementary but separate concerns. The reference concentrates on participant protection, access, equipment, privacy, and recruitment power, while the compared frame concentrates on field-evaluation measures, operational decision rules, workload redistribution, adoption, fidelity, and longitudinal measurement conditions.

relations.reason: This is a one-sided participant-protection control with no corresponding operational claim in the compared frame.
relations.summary: Participant burdens and mitigations are linked task by task and checked by HCI ethics reviewers.

relations.reason: These memories split one accessibility-support requirement covering both accommodation identification and provision; the compared frame has no counterpart.
relations.summary: Necessary accessibility accommodations and their delivery during study sessions must be specified.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful one-sided privacy procedure absent from the compared frame.
relations.summary: Personal identifiers are separated from research data immediately after collection.

relations.reason: These memories split one equipment-access arrangement; the compared frame does not address participant device loans.
relations.summary: Necessary participant equipment loans cover both the devices supplied and their return procedure.

relations.reason: This is a distinct one-sided expectation-setting safeguard with no compared-frame counterpart.
relations.summary: Participants are told that the formative prototype is not a finished service.

relations.reason: This participant-burden limit is independent of the compared frame's observation about changing measurement conditions over time.
relations.summary: Repeated evaluations involving the same participant are subject to an upper limit on cumulative task burden.

relations.reason: This is a distinct one-sided observation about proposal framing and does not correspond to any compared-frame evaluation policy.
relations.summary: The proposal author tends to emphasize expected prototype benefits over participant burden.

relations.reason: This is a distinct one-sided recruitment power condition absent from the compared frame.
relations.summary: Organizational recruitment authority and academic or professional evaluation authority may be combined in one leadership or staff role.

relations.reason: These memories split one operational measurement-governance framework; the reference frame contains no corresponding deployment decision rule.
relations.summary: Deployment decisions use a representative primary measure, declared decision thresholds, and review of whether that measure supports maintain, modify, or discontinue choices.

relations.reason: This is a distinct one-sided organizational workload assessment, not a participant task-burden safeguard.
relations.summary: Design changes are evaluated for whether workload reductions in one role create new tasks for other roles.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful one-sided outcome distinction absent from the reference frame.
relations.summary: Usability and organizational adoption intent are treated as separate evaluation outcomes.

relations.reason: This is a distinct one-sided field-implementation concept with no reference-frame counterpart.
relations.summary: Implementation fidelity assesses whether planned features and operational procedures were delivered in the field as intended.

relations.reason: This is a distinct one-sided measurement-validity qualification rather than a rule governing cumulative participant burden.
relations.summary: Initial evaluation and long-term operation have different measurement conditions because exposure duration and repeated-use frequency differ.

reports.compared_only: Compared-only content covers metric-led deployment decisions, workload redistribution, distinct adoption outcomes, implementation fidelity, and measurement differences between initial and long-term use.
reports.reference_only: Reference-only content covers task burden safeguards, accessibility delivery, device loans, de-identification, prototype disclosure, repeated-study limits, benefit-framing bias, and recruitment power.
